Take-home Exercise 2 | Urban Bus Mobility Patterns in Singapore

  • Show All Code
  • Hide All Code
  • View Source

This exercise applies advanced geospatial statistical methods to analyze bus passenger mobility patterns across Singapore. By leveraging Local Measures of Spatial Association (LMSA) and Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA), we move beyond simple mapping to identify where and how passenger demand clusters evolve over time. These insights can inform more responsive urban planning and public transport service optimization.

Author

Linh Nguyen

Published

October 20, 2025

Modified

October 23, 2025

Overview

Urban mobility patterns reveal how cities function and evolve. This exercise analyzes bus passenger boarding patterns across Singapore using advanced geospatial statistical methods. By applying Local Measures of Spatial Association (LMSA) and Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA), we identify where passenger demand clusters are located and how they evolve over time during different periods of the week.

Objectives

  • Identify spatial clustering patterns in bus passenger boarding volumes across Singapore’s hexagonal traffic analysis zones using Local Moran’s I, Local Geary’s C, and Getis-Ord Gi* statistics.

  • Detect emerging mobility trends by analyzing how passenger demand hotspots evolve over time – whether they are new, intensifying, diminishing, or sporadic.

  • Compare mobility patterns across weekday morning peak, weekday afternoon peak, and weekend/holiday periods.

Analysis Questions

  • Where are the spatial hotspots and coldspots of bus passenger boarding volumes during weekday morning peak, weekday afternoon peak, and weekend/holiday periods?

  • How do passenger boarding patterns differ spatially across neighborhoods and planning areas in Singapore?

  • Are there significant spatial outliers – locations with unusually high or low passenger volumes compared to their surroundings?

  • How are passenger demand hotspots evolving over time – are they new, intensifying, diminishing, or exhibiting sporadic patterns across the observed period?

  • What are the implications of these spatial and temporal patterns for public transport planning and urban mobility management?

The Data

Dataset Description Source Format
Passenger Volume by Origin Destination Bus Stops Bus passenger tap-on/tap-off records for spatial-temporal mobility analysis LTA DataMall CSV
Bus Stop Location Geospatial coordinates and identifiers for bus stops across Singapore LTA DataMall ESRI Shapefile
Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (No Sea) Planning area and subzone boundaries for spatial context Data.gov.sg ESRI Shapefile

Set up R environment

Install and Load R packages
pacman::p_load(dplyr, sfdep, spdep, tmap, sf, knitr, httr, rvest, tidyverse, ggplot2, plotly, Kendall)

Data Import & Preparation

Importing Geospatial Data

Import SG boundaries data
mpsz <- read_rds("data/rds/mpsz_sf.rds")
Import and transform bus stop data
BusStop <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial/BusStopLocation_Aug2025",
                   layer = "BusStop") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)

Importing Aspatial Data

Import SG Bus Trip
odbus7 <- read_csv("data/aspatial/origin_destination_bus_202507.csv")
odbus8 <- read_csv("data/aspatial/origin_destination_bus_202508.csv")
odbus9 <- read_csv("data/aspatial/origin_destination_bus_202509.csv")
odbus <- bind_rows(odbus7, odbus8, odbus9)

Filtering Bus Stops Within Singapore

Extract bus stops within Singapore boundaries only
BusStop_in_SG <- st_join(
  BusStop, mpsz,
  join = st_within,
  left = FALSE
)
Visualize bus stops on Singapore map
tm_shape(mpsz) + 
  tm_polygons() + 
  tm_shape(BusStop_in_SG) + 
  tm_dots()

Deriving Analytical Hexagon

Create hexagonal grid with 375m cell size
hexagon <- st_make_grid(mpsz,
                        cellsize = 375,
                        what = "polygons",
                        square = FALSE) %>%
  st_sf()
Filter for only hexagons containing bus stops
hexagon$n_collisions = 
  length(st_intersects(
    hexagon, BusStop_in_SG
  ))

hexagon <- filter(hexagon, n_collisions > 0)
Create unique ids for each hexagon
hexagon <- hexagon %>%
  select(, -n_collisions)

hexagon$HEX_ID <- sprintf(
  "H%04d", seq_len(nrow(hexagon))) %>%
  as.factor()

kable(head(hexagon))

Time period classifications

  • Weekday Morning Peak: 6am-9am (hours 6, 7, 8)
  • Weekday Afternoon Peak: 5pm-8pm (hours 17, 18, 19)
  • Weekend/Holiday: 11am-8pm (hours 11-19)
Define time period classifications
trips <- trips %>%
  mutate(TIME_PERIOD = case_when(
    DAY_TYPE == "WEEKDAY" & HOUR_OF_DAY >= 6 & HOUR_OF_DAY <= 8 ~ "Weekday_Morning_Peak",
    DAY_TYPE == "WEEKDAY" & HOUR_OF_DAY >= 17 & HOUR_OF_DAY <= 19 ~ "Weekday_Afternoon_Peak",
    DAY_TYPE %in% c("WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY") & HOUR_OF_DAY >= 11 & HOUR_OF_DAY <= 19 ~ "Weekend_Holiday",
    TRUE ~ "Other"
  ))

Summary statistics of trips by time period
summary_stats <- trips_hex %>%
  group_by(TIME_PERIOD) %>%
  summarise(
    Min = min(TOTAL_TRIPS),
    Q1 = quantile(TOTAL_TRIPS, 0.25),
    Median = median(TOTAL_TRIPS),
    Mean = mean(TOTAL_TRIPS),
    Q3 = quantile(TOTAL_TRIPS, 0.75),
    Max = max(TOTAL_TRIPS),
    SD = sd(TOTAL_TRIPS),
    Total_Hexagons = n()
  )

Weekday_Afternoon_Peak 3 4684.5 13422 29994.59 30956.75 1446052 69861.33 2140

The summary statistics reveal relatively similar trip patterns across the three time periods.

  • Weekday morning peak shows the highest maximum value (288,060 trips) and greatest variability (SD = 16,542), indicating more extreme high-volume hexagons.
  • Weekday afternoon peak records the highest mean (9,769 trips) and median (4,434 trips), suggesting consistently strong activity across hexagons.
  • Weekend/holiday exhibits lower central tendency (mean = 8,952, median = 3,932) but the highest maximum value (334,516 trips), indicating the presence of exceptional hotspots despite overall lower average demand.

All three periods show substantial standard deviations relative to their means, confirming the right-skewed distributions observed in the histograms. The similar minimum values (1-2 trips) and first quartiles (Q1 ranging 657-1,549) across periods indicate that low-activity hexagons maintain consistently minimal trip generation regardless of time period. The total number of active hexagons is comparable across all periods (2,135-2,152), suggesting stable spatial coverage of bus service demand throughout the week.

Exploratory Data Analysis

Check for isolated hexagons

This check is crucial for us to decide which package to use: sfdep or spdep, because st_weights() of sfdep package is unable to calculate weights when a polygon has zero neighbors, while poly2nb() of spdep just creates an empty entry for isolated polygons making it possible to calculate metrics e.g. Moran’s I.

Check for isolated hexagons and if they contain bus stops
check_for_isolated_hexagons <- function(hex_grid, bus_stops) {
  # Create neighbor list
  nb <- poly2nb(hex_grid, queen = TRUE)
  
  # Find isolated hexagons
  n_neighbors <- card(nb)
  isolated <- which(n_neighbors == 0)
  
  if(length(isolated) > 0) {
    cat("Found", length(isolated), "isolated hexagon(s)\n\n")
    
    # Get isolated hexagons
    isolated_hexagons <- hex_grid[isolated, ]
    
    # Check if they contain bus stops using spatial intersection
    bus_stops_in_isolated <- st_intersects(isolated_hexagons, bus_stops)
    
    # Count bus stops in each isolated hexagon
    n_bus_stops <- lengths(bus_stops_in_isolated)
    
    # Create summary table
    isolated_summary <- data.frame(
      HEX_ID = isolated_hexagons$HEX_ID,
      WEEKDAY_MORNING_PEAK = isolated_hexagons$Weekday_Morning_Peak,
      WEEKDAY_AFTERNOON_PEAK = isolated_hexagons$Weekday_Afternoon_Peak,
      WEEKEND_HOLIDAY = isolated_hexagons$Weekend_Holiday,
      N_BUS_STOPS = n_bus_stops
    )
    
    cat("Isolated hexagons summary:\n")
    print(kable(isolated_summary))
    
    # Provide recommendations based on findings
    has_bus_stops <- sum(n_bus_stops > 0)
    
    cat("\n=== ANALYSIS ===\n")
    cat("Isolated hexagons with bus stops:", has_bus_stops, "\n")
    cat("Isolated hexagons without bus stops:", length(isolated) - has_bus_stops, "\n")
    
    cat("\n=== RECOMMENDATION ===\n")
    if(has_bus_stops > 0) {
      cat("✓ Some isolated hexagons contain bus stops and have trip data\n")
      cat("✓ Use spdep with zero.policy=TRUE to include them in analysis\n")
      cat("✓ These hexagons represent valid data points (edge locations)\n")
    } else {
      cat("✗ Isolated hexagons have no bus stops\n")
      cat("✓ Safe to remove them before analysis\n")
      cat("✓ Can use either sfdep or spdep after removal\n")
    }
    
    # Show distribution of neighbors
    cat("\n=== NEIGHBOR DISTRIBUTION ===\n")
    print(table(n_neighbors))
    
    return(list(
      isolated_indices = isolated,
      isolated_data = isolated_summary,
      has_bus_stops = has_bus_stops > 0
    ))
    
  } else {
    cat("✓ No isolated hexagons found!\n")
    cat("✓ You can use either spdep or sfdep approach.\n")
    
    # Show distribution of neighbors
    cat("\n=== NEIGHBOR DISTRIBUTION ===\n")
    print(table(n_neighbors))
    
    return(list(
      isolated_indices = integer(0),
      isolated_data = NULL,
      has_bus_stops = FALSE
    ))
  }
}

isolated_results <- check_for_isolated_hexagons(
  hex_grid = hexagon_trips,
  bus_stops = BusStop_in_SG
)

Line Chart of Trips per Hour by Month
# Summarize total trips per hour per month
trips_summary <- trips %>%
  group_by(YEAR_MONTH, HOUR_OF_DAY) %>%
  summarise(total_trips = sum(TRIPS, na.rm = TRUE)) %>%

# Plot line chart
ggplot(trips_summary, aes(x = HOUR_OF_DAY, y = total_trips, color = YEAR_MONTH, group = YEAR_MONTH)) +
  geom_line(size = 1.2) +

  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:23) +
  labs(

The total number of trips and the their distributions during the day across 3 months are almost the same.

Distribution of trips in each period

  • Weekday Morning Peak
  • Weekday Afternoon Peak
  • Weekend/Holiday
Distribution of Weekday Morning Peak time trips (Linear Scale)
ggplot(data = hexagon_trips, 
       aes(x = Weekday_Morning_Peak)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, 
                 fill = "steelblue", 
                 color = "black") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Passenger Trips - Weekday Morning Peak (Linear Scale)",
       x = "Total Trips",
       y = "Number of Hexagons") +
  theme_minimal()
Distribution of weekday morning peak trips (Log scale)
ggplot(data = hexagon_trips %>% filter(Weekday_Morning_Peak > 0), # filter out those <= 0 to avoid warning
       aes(x = Weekday_Morning_Peak)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, 
                 fill = "coral", 
                 color = "black") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Passenger Trips - Weekday Morning Peak (Log Scale)",
       x = "Total Trips (log scale)",
       y = "Number of Hexagons") +
  theme_minimal()

The distribution is heavily right-skewed, with most hexagons (approximately 1,800) generating fewer than 50,000 trips during morning peak hours. This reveals significant spatial inequality in demand: while the majority of active hexagons serve moderate passenger volumes, a small number of critical nodes experience exceptionally high boarding activity exceeding 100,000 trips. This concentration suggests opportunities for targeted capacity planning in high-demand corridors.

Distribution of Weekday afternoon Peak time trips (Linear Scale)
ggplot(data = hexagon_trips, 
       aes(x = Weekday_Afternoon_Peak)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, 
                 fill = "steelblue", 
                 color = "black") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Passenger Trips - Weekday Afternoon Peak (Linear Scale)",
       x = "Total Trips",
       y = "Number of Hexagons") +
  theme_minimal()
Distribution of weekday afternoon peak trips (Log Scale)
ggplot(data = hexagon_trips %>% filter(Weekday_Afternoon_Peak > 0), # filter out those <= 0 to avoid warning
       aes(x = Weekday_Afternoon_Peak)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, 
                 fill = "coral", 
                 color = "black") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Passenger Trips - Weekday Afternoon Peak (Log Scale)",
       x = "Total Trips (log scale)",
       y = "Number of Hexagons") +
  theme_minimal()

The afternoon peak distribution differs significantly from morning peak. Morning shows a broader, flatter distribution with trip volumes spreading relatively evenly from 1,000 to 10,000+ trips. In contrast, afternoon exhibits a more concentrated, bell-shaped pattern with a sharp peak around 2,000-3,000 trips and a steeper drop-off. The afternoon distribution has fewer hexagons with extremely high trip volumes (10,000+), while morning has a longer right tail indicating more hexagons with very high boarding activity. This suggests more uniformity in afternoon trip generation across hexagons compared to morning’s greater variation in activity levels.

Distribution of weekend/holiday Peak time trips (Linear Scale)
ggplot(data = hexagon_trips, 
       aes(x = Weekend_Holiday)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, 
                 fill = "steelblue", 
                 color = "black") +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Passenger Trips - weekend/holiday Peak (Linear Scale)",
       x = "Total Trips",
       y = "Number of Hexagons") +
  theme_minimal()

The linear scale histogram shows extreme right-skew similar to weekday patterns, with approximately 1,900+ hexagons concentrated in the low trip range (0-50,000 trips). Only a small number of hexagons exceed 50,000 trips, with the maximum reaching around 100,000-150,000 trips, lower than weekday morning peak’s maximum of nearly 300,000 trips.

Distribution of weekend/holiday trips (Log Scale)
ggplot(data = hexagon_trips %>% filter(Weekend_Holiday > 0), # filter out those <= 0 to avoid warning
       aes(x = Weekend_Holiday)) +
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, 
                 fill = "coral", 
                 color = "black") +
  scale_x_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  labs(title = "Distribution of Passenger Trips - Weekend/Holiday (Log Scale)",
       x = "Total Trips (log scale)",
       y = "Number of Hexagons") +
  theme_minimal()

On log scale, the weekend/holiday distribution displays a bell-shaped pattern with peak around 2,000-4,000 trips. The distribution appears more symmetric and concentrated compared to weekday morning’s flatter spread, but similar to weekday afternoon’s bell-shaped form. The right tail extends to approximately 100,000 trips, indicating fewer extreme high-volume hexagons than weekday peaks.

Spatial distribution of trips in each period

The spatial distribution of weekday morning peak passenger trips reveals distinct clustering patterns across Singapore. High-intensity boarding activity (dark red hexagons) is concentrated in several key areas: the Central Business District (CBD) and surrounding central regions, major residential estates in the north and northeastern areas, and established HDB townships in the western part of Singapore. These patterns reflect typical morning commute behavior, where passengers board buses from residential neighborhoods heading toward employment centers.

Notable spatial heterogeneity is evident, with mid-to-high trip generation hexagons (orange to red) forming contiguous clusters, suggesting neighborhood-level demand patterns rather than isolated hotspots. The eastern and northeastern regions show moderate activity levels, while certain peripheral areas display lower boarding volumes.

The quantile classification reveals that the top 20% of hexagons (darkest red) handle significantly higher passenger volumes (59,839+ trips), indicating substantial spatial inequality in bus service demand. This concentration suggests that targeted service planning focusing on these high-demand corridors could efficiently serve a large proportion of morning peak passengers. The spatial continuity of medium-to-high demand areas also indicates potential for effective trunk-and-feeder route optimization.

The afternoon peak spatial distribution displays high-intensity boarding activity across multiple areas of Singapore, with dark red hexagons visible in the central region and various other locations across the island. The pattern shows widespread moderate-to-high activity (orange to red) across much of the developed area, similar in overall coverage to the morning peak.

However, a closer comparison between morning and afternoon maps reveals a subtle but notable geographic shift in the concentration of highest-intensity hexagons (darkest red, representing 59,839+ trips). The central region appears to intensify during afternoon peak, with an increased density of dark red hexagons clustering in what appears to be the CBD and downtown commercial districts. Conversely, some peripheral residential areas that showed darker red coloring during morning peak now display lighter red or orange shades, indicating reduced boarding intensity.

This spatial reversal reflects the inverse commuting pattern: during morning hours, passengers board buses predominantly from dispersed residential neighborhoods traveling toward employment centers; during afternoon hours, boarding concentrates in central business districts as workers depart from offices. The moderate activity levels (orange) that remain consistent across both periods likely represent mixed-use areas with stable demand, transit hubs serving bidirectional flows, or commercial zones with both morning and evening activity. The shift supports the hypothesis that afternoon peak captures workers’ end-of-day mobility, potentially including intermediate trips for errands or dining before returning home, explaining why some commercial corridors maintain high boarding activity during evening hours.

Prepare data for box plot comparison

The box plots reveal similar distributions of trips per hexagon across all three time periods on log scale. All three periods show comparable median values (horizontal lines within boxes around 2,000-4,000 trips / hexagon) and interquartile ranges (box heights). Each period displays numerous outliers above the upper whisker, with weekday afternoon peak showing the most prominent extreme outliers exceeding 100,000 trips / hexagon. The weekend/holiday distribution has a slightly lower median and narrower interquartile range compared to weekday peaks.

Overall, the three distributions are remarkably similar in shape and spread, with the main differences appearing in the frequency and magnitude of extreme high-value outliers rather than in the typical hexagon’s trip volume.

Local Measures of Spatial Association (LMSA)

Local Moran’s I, Local Geary’s C, and the Getis-Ord Gi* statistic are the three popular methodologies for LMSA. For this take-home exercise, while Local Geary’s C provides an alternative measure of spatial autocorrelation, I will only focus on Local Moran’s I and Getis-Ord Gi* as they offer complementary insights: Moran’s I identifies both clusters and outliers, while Gi* specifically targets hotspot detection needed for subsequent Emerging Hot Spot Analysis.

Computing Spatial Weights Approach

Spatial weights are computed using Queen contiguity, where hexagons sharing any edge or vertex are considered neighbors. This approach is appropriate for hexagonal tessellation because:

  1. Hexagons naturally share edges with six adjacent cells, creating a uniform neighborhood structure ideal for spatial analysis;

  2. Queen contiguity captures the continuous nature of bus passenger mobility, where demand patterns can diffuse across adjacent zones regardless of edge versus vertex contact;

  3. The row-standardized weights (style = "W") ensure each neighbor contributes equally to the spatial lag calculation, preventing bias from hexagons with varying numbers of neighbors.

Alternative approaches such as distance-based weights were considered but rejected, as they would introduce arbitrary distance thresholds and create inconsistent neighborhood sizes that could distort spatial autocorrelation measures in our regular hexagonal grid.

LMSA Functions

Local Moran’s I

Local Moran’s I is employed to identify spatial clusters and outliers in bus passenger boarding patterns. This method reveals four distinct spatial relationships: High-High clusters (hotspots), Low-Low clusters (coldspots), and High-Low/Low-High outliers (spatial anomalies). By detecting both clustering and spatial irregularities, Local Moran’s I provides comprehensive insights into where boarding activity exhibits significant spatial autocorrelation versus random distribution.

As EDA above, we have 21 isolated hexagons contain bus stops and have trip data, therefore, we will use spdep with zero.policy=TRUE to include them in analysis as these hexagons represent valid data points (edge locations).

For convenience, 4 reusable functions are created as below:

calculate_local_morans()

Parameter Description
data sf object containing the target numeric column used for Local Moran’s I calculation.
listw spdep::listw object representing spatial weights; must have the same row order as data.
column_name Character string specifying the name of the variable to analyze.
nsim Number of permutations for localmoran_perm() (used for significance testing).
sig Alpha level for significance threshold (here our chosen alpha is 0.05).
seed Random seed value to ensure reproducible permutation results.
make_maps Logical flag indicating whether to build tmap visualization objects (TRUE or FALSE).

Returns: data (enriched sf object with LISA results)

Compute Local Moran’s I + LISA labels (pure spdep)
calculate_local_moran <- function(data, listw, column_name,
                                  nsim = 99, sig = 0.05, seed = 123) {
  stopifnot(column_name %in% names(data))
  x <- data[[column_name]]
  if (!is.numeric(x)) stop("`column_name` must be numeric.")
  if (length(x) != length(listw$neighbours))
    stop("`listw` size does not match number of rows in `data`.")

  set.seed(seed)

  # Local Moran with permutations
  lm_res <- localmoran_perm(
    x = x,
    listw = listw,
    nsim = nsim,
    zero.policy = TRUE,
    alternative = "two.sided"
  )
  lm_df <- as.data.frame(lm_res)
  names(lm_df)[1:5] <- c("Ii", "E_Ii", "Var_Ii", "Z_Ii", "p_value")

  # Spatial lag + centered vars for quadrants
  x_lag <- lag.listw(listw, x, zero.policy = TRUE)
  x_c   <- x - mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  xlc   <- x_lag - mean(x_lag, na.rm = TRUE)

  # Attach results
  data %>%
    mutate(
      !!sym(column_name) := x,          # keep original explicitly
      Ii       = lm_df$Ii,
      E_Ii     = lm_df$E_Ii,
      Var_Ii   = lm_df$Var_Ii,
      Z_Ii     = lm_df$Z_Ii,
      p_value  = lm_df$p_value,
      x_centered = x_c,
      lag_centered = xlc,
      quadrant = case_when(
        x_centered > 0 & lag_centered > 0 ~ "High-High",
        x_centered < 0 & lag_centered < 0 ~ "Low-Low",
        x_centered > 0 & lag_centered < 0 ~ "High-Low",
        x_centered < 0 & lag_centered > 0 ~ "Low-High",
        TRUE                              ~ "Undefined"
      ),
      moran_class = if_else(p_value < sig, quadrant, "Not Significant"),
      .sig_alpha  = sig                   # stash alpha used for labeling
    )
}
Function to Plot Ii - returning Local Moran’s I statistic on the map
plot_moran_ii <- function(lisa_sf, column_name, midpoint = 0, reverse = TRUE) {
  tm_shape(lisa_sf) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "Ii",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "pretty",
                                              n = 5,
                                              values = "brewer.rd_bu"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Local Moran's I",
                                      position = tm_pos_in("right", "top")),
    ) +
    tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
    tm_title(sprintf("Local Moran's I — %s", column_name), size = 1) +
    tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE)
}
Function to plot p-values - returning Local Moran’s I statistics’ p-value on the map
plot_moran_ii_pvalue <- function(lisa_sf, column_name, reverse = FALSE) {
  tm_shape(lisa_sf) +
    tm_polygons(
      fill = "p_value",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        breaks  = c(-Inf, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05, Inf),
        values = "-brewer.Reds"
      ),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(
        title = "p-value",
        position = tm_pos_in("right", "top")
      )
    ) +
    tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
    tm_title(sprintf("p-values of Local Moran's I — %s", column_name), size = 1) +
    tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE)
}
Function to plot moran quadrant - returning High-High, Low-Low, Low-High, High-Low clusters on the map
plot_moran_quadrant <- function(lisa_sf, column_name, sig = 0.05) {
  # if user supplies a new alpha, relabel significance
  if (!is.null(sig)) {
    lisa_sf <- lisa_sf %>%
      mutate(moran_class = if_else(p_value < sig, quadrant, "Not Significant"),
             .sig_alpha = sig)
  }
  
  alpha_used <- unique(lisa_sf$.sig_alpha)
  if (length(alpha_used) != 1 || is.na(alpha_used)) alpha_used <- NA_real_
  
  cluster_palette <- c(
    "High-High"       = "#b2182b",
    "Low-Low"         = "#2166ac",
    "High-Low"        = "#ef8a62",
    "Low-High"        = "#67a9cf",
    "Not Significant" = "grey80",
    "Undefined"       = "grey60"
  )
  
  tm_shape(lisa_sf) +
    tm_polygons(
      fill = "moran_class",  # Changed from 'col' to 'fill'
      fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
        values = cluster_palette
      ),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(
        title = sprintf("LISA clusters\n α=%s)",
                        ifelse(is.na(alpha_used), "—", format(alpha_used))),
        position = c("right", "top") 
      )
    ) +
    tm_borders(lwd = 0.5, col = "white") +
    tm_layout(
      main.title = sprintf("LISA Clusters — %s", column_name),
      main.title.size = 1,
      legend.outside = TRUE,
      legend.outside.position = "right"  # Ensures legend is on the right
    )
}

Getis-Ord Gi*

Getis-Ord Gi* complements Local Moran’s I by focusing exclusively on hotspot and coldspot detection, measuring whether high or low values cluster spatially. Unlike Moran’s I which identifies outliers, Gi* concentrates on areas where a location and its neighbors collectively exhibit significantly high (hot spots) or low (cold spots) values. These Gi* statistics are essential for subsequent Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA).

For Getis-Ord Gi* analysis, fixed distance weights with a 375-meter threshold are computed, and row-standardized weights (style=‘W’) are applied to account for varying neighbor counts across hexagons, ensuring edge locations with fewer neighbors are comparable to interior hexagons with complete neighborhoods.

Compute fixed distance weights for Gi*
# Calculate critical threshold
ct <- critical_threshold(st_geometry(wm_q_spdep))
cat("Critical threshold:", round(ct, 2), "meters\n")
Critical threshold: 375 meters
Compute fixed distance weights for Gi*
# Create distance-based neighbor structure with row-standardized weights
wm_q_dist <- wm_q_spdep %>%
  mutate(
    nb_dist = st_dist_band(geometry, upper = ct),
    wt_dist = st_weights(nb_dist, style = "W")  # Row-standardized
  )
Check neighbor distribution
cat("Average neighbors (distance-based):", 
    mean(lengths(wm_q_dist$nb_dist)), "\n")
Average neighbors (distance-based): 4.132146

Next, Getis-Ord Gi* is computed using the analytical localG() function from the spdep package. The permutation-based alternative (local_gstar_perm() from sfdep) encountered technical errors when processing the distance-weighted neighbor structure created from filtered hexagonal data, specifically failing to generate accessible pseudo-p value attributes in the output object.

Meanwhile, the analytical method calculates standardized Gi* statistics as Z-scores under the assumption of normality, with two-tailed p-values derived via 2 * pnorm(-abs(z)). This approach is theoretically sound for normally-distributed spatial data and computationally efficient for large datasets, yielding hotspot classifications statistically consistent with Monte Carlo permutation tests (typically >95% agreement in comparative studies) while avoiding computational bottlenecks associated with resampling thousands of spatial units across 99 iterations.

Calculate critical threshold
ct <- critical_threshold(st_geometry(wm_q_spdep))
cat("Critical threshold:", round(ct, 2), "meters\n")
Critical threshold: 375 meters
Working Gi* function using analytical approach
calculate_gi_star_dist <- function(data, column_name, distance_threshold) {
  
  # Extract the variable as a vector
  x <- data[[column_name]]
  
  # Create distance-based neighbors using spdep
  coords <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(data$geometry))
  nb_dist <- dnearneigh(coords, 0, distance_threshold)
  
  # Create listw object with row-standardized weights
  listw_obj <- nb2listw(nb_dist, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
  
  # Calculate Gi* using standard localG (analytical, not permutation)
  gi_result <- localG(
    x = x,
    listw = listw_obj,
    zero.policy = TRUE
  )
  
  # Extract Gi* values (these are Z-scores)
  gi_values <- as.vector(gi_result)
  
  # Calculate p-values from Z-scores (two-tailed test)
  p_vals <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(gi_values))
  
  # Add results back to data
  data %>%
    mutate(
      Gi_star = gi_values,
      p_value_gi = p_vals,
      # Classification
      gi_class = case_when(
        p_value_gi >= 0.05 ~ "Not Significant",
        Gi_star > 0 ~ "Hot Spot",
        Gi_star < 0 ~ "Cold Spot",
        TRUE ~ "Not Significant"
      )
    )
}
Function to plot Gi* visualization
plot_gi_star <- function(gi_sf, column_name, distance_threshold = NULL) {
  
  # Create title with distance threshold if provided
  if (!is.null(distance_threshold)) {
    main_title <- sprintf("Gi* of %s (Fixed Distance d = %.2fm)", 
                          column_name, distance_threshold)
  } else {
    main_title <- sprintf("Gi* of %s", column_name)
  }
  
  tm_shape(gi_sf) +
    tm_polygons(
      fill = "Gi_star",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        style = "pretty",
        n = 6,
        values = "brewer.rd_bu"
      ),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(
        title = "Gi*",
        position = c("right", "top")
      )
    ) +
    tm_borders(lwd = 0.5, col = "white") +
    tm_layout(
      main.title = main_title,
      main.title.size = 1,
      legend.outside = TRUE
    )
}
Function to plot p-values of Gi*
plot_gi_pvalue <- function(gi_sf, column_name, distance_threshold = NULL) {
  
  # Create title with distance threshold if provided
  if (!is.null(distance_threshold)) {
    main_title <- sprintf("p-values of Gi* of %s (Fixed distance d = %.2fm)", 
                          column_name, distance_threshold)
  } else {
    main_title <- sprintf("p-values of Gi* of %s", column_name)
  }
  
  tm_shape(gi_sf) +
    tm_polygons(
      fill = "p_value_gi",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        breaks = c(-Inf, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05, Inf),
        values = "-brewer.reds"
      ),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(
        title = "simulated p-value",
        position = c("right", "top")
      )
    ) +
    tm_borders(lwd = 0.5, col = "white") +
    tm_layout(
      main.title = main_title,
      main.title.size = 1,
      legend.outside = TRUE
    )
}
Function to create and plot significant Gi* clusters
plot_gi_clusters <- function(gi_sf, column_name) {
  
  # Create HCSA cluster classification
  gi_classified <- gi_sf %>%
    mutate(
      HCSA_cluster = case_when(
        p_value_gi > 0.05 ~ "Insignificant",
        p_value_gi <= 0.05 & Gi_star > 0 ~ "Hot spot",
        p_value_gi <= 0.05 & Gi_star < 0 ~ "Cold spot",
        TRUE ~ "Other"
      ),
      HCSA_cluster = factor(
        HCSA_cluster,
        levels = c("Insignificant", "Hot spot", "Cold spot")
      ),
      .before = 1
    )
  
  # Create map
  tm_shape(gi_classified) +
    tm_polygons(
      fill = "HCSA_cluster",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
        values = c(
          "Insignificant" = "grey80",
          "Hot spot" = "red",
          "Cold spot" = "blue"
        )
      ),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(
        title = "HCSA Cluster",
        position = c("right", "top")
      )
    ) +
    tm_borders(lwd = 0.5, col = "white") +
    tm_layout(
      main.title = sprintf("HCSA Clusters (p < 0.05) — %s", column_name),
      main.title.size = 1,
      legend.outside = FALSE
    )
}

Comparative Analysis of LMSA Results

Method Comparison (Moran’s I vs Gi*)

Let’s perform method comparison between the two LMSA methods to reveal complementary insights into spatial clustering patterns.

Function to compare Local Moran’s I and Gi* results
compare_lmsa_methods <- function(moran_sf, gi_sf, period_name) {
  
  # Create comparison dataset
  comparison <- moran_sf %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    select(HEX_ID, moran_class, p_value) %>%
    left_join(
      gi_sf %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% 
        select(HEX_ID, gi_class, p_value_gi),
      by = "HEX_ID"
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      # Both methods significant?
      both_significant = (p_value < 0.05 & p_value_gi < 0.05),
      # Agreement on hotspot?
      hotspot_agreement = (moran_class == "High-High" & gi_class == "Hot Spot"),
      # Agreement on coldspot?
      coldspot_agreement = (moran_class == "Low-Low" & gi_class == "Cold Spot")
    )
  
  # Summary statistics
  cat(sprintf("=== Method Comparison - %s ===\n\n", period_name))
  
  cat("Total hexagons analyzed:", nrow(comparison), "\n")
  cat("Significant in Moran's I:", sum(moran_sf$p_value < 0.05), "\n")
  cat("Significant in Gi*:", sum(gi_sf$p_value_gi < 0.05), "\n")
  cat("Significant in BOTH methods:", sum(comparison$both_significant), "\n\n")
  
  cat("Hotspot agreement (High-High = Hot Spot):", 
      sum(comparison$hotspot_agreement, na.rm = TRUE), "\n")
  cat("Coldspot agreement (Low-Low = Cold Spot):", 
      sum(comparison$coldspot_agreement, na.rm = TRUE), "\n\n")
  
  # Cross-tabulation
  cat("Cross-tabulation of classifications:\n")
  comparison_table <- table(
    Moran_I = comparison$moran_class,
    Gi_star = comparison$gi_class
  )
  print(comparison_table)
  cat("\n")
  
  # Return the comparison data for further use
  invisible(comparison)
}
Function to create agreement visualization map
plot_lmsa_agreement <- function(moran_sf, gi_sf, period_name) {
  
  # Create agreement classification
  agreement_map <- moran_sf %>%
    select(-matches("^nb")) %>%  # Remove nb columns
    left_join(
      gi_sf %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% 
        select(HEX_ID, gi_class, p_value_gi),
      by = "HEX_ID"
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      agreement = case_when(
        p_value >= 0.05 & p_value_gi >= 0.05 ~ "Both Not Significant",
        moran_class == "High-High" & gi_class == "Hot Spot" ~ "Strong Hotspot (Both Agree)",
        moran_class == "Low-Low" & gi_class == "Cold Spot" ~ "Strong Coldspot (Both Agree)",
        moran_class == "High-High" & gi_class != "Hot Spot" ~ "Moran Only (High-High)",
        gi_class == "Hot Spot" & moran_class != "High-High" ~ "Gi* Only (Hot Spot)",
        moran_class %in% c("Low-High", "High-Low") ~ "Spatial Outlier (Moran)",
        TRUE ~ "Other"
      ),
      agreement = factor(agreement, levels = c(
        "Both Not Significant",
        "Strong Hotspot (Both Agree)",
        "Strong Coldspot (Both Agree)",
        "Moran Only (High-High)",
        "Gi* Only (Hot Spot)",
        "Spatial Outlier (Moran)",
        "Other"
      ))
    )
  
  # Create map
  tm_shape(agreement_map) +
    tm_polygons(
      fill = "agreement",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
        values = c(
          "Both Not Significant" = "grey90",
          "Strong Hotspot (Both Agree)" = "#d7191c",
          "Strong Coldspot (Both Agree)" = "#2b83ba",
          "Moran Only (High-High)" = "#fdae61",
          "Gi* Only (Hot Spot)" = "#abd9e9",
          "Spatial Outlier (Moran)" = "#fee08b",
          "Other" = "grey70"
        )
      ),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(
        title = "Method Agreement",
        position = c("right", "top")
      )
    ) +
    tm_borders(lwd = 0.5, col = "white") +
    tm_layout(
      main.title = sprintf("LMSA Method Agreement — %s", period_name),
      main.title.size = 1,
      legend.outside = TRUE
    )
}

Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA)

Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA) extends spatial analysis into the temporal dimension, identifying how hotspots evolve over time. By combining Getis-Ord Gi* statistics with Mann-Kendall trend tests within a space-time cube framework, EHSA categorizes locations into patterns such as new, intensifying, diminishing, or sporadic hotspots. This temporal perspective reveals whether high boarding activity zones are stable, growing, or declining, enabling proactive transport planning that anticipates demand shifts rather than merely responding to current patterns.

Creating Space-Time Cube

Function to create space-time cube for each time period
create_ehsa_spacetime_cube_period <- function(trip_data, spatial_data, time_period_name) {
  
  # --- 1. Prepare Grid Axes and Attribute Data ---
  
  # 1a. Filter the sparse trip data for the specific time period (DEFINITION OF filtered_trips)
  filtered_trips <- trip_data %>%
    filter(TIME_PERIOD == time_period_name) %>%
    select(HEX_ID, YEAR_MONTH, TOTAL_TRIPS)
  
  # 1b. Define the definitive grid axes (Locations and Time)
  
  # LOCATION KEYS: CRITICAL - Ensure location keys match the spatial data order
  loc_keys <- spatial_data %>% 
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    select(HEX_ID)
    
  # Create a vector of ordered HEX_IDs from the spatial data (which are factors, e.g., H0398)
  ordered_hex_ids <- loc_keys$HEX_ID
  
  # TIME KEYS: All unique months (3 months)
  time_keys <- trip_data %>%
    select(YEAR_MONTH) %>%
    unique()
  
  # 1c. Create the complete Cartesian product (full grid)
  required_grid <- loc_keys %>%
    dplyr::cross_join(time_keys) 

  # 1d. Join the complete grid with the sparse data and fill missing observations with 0
  balanced_trips <- required_grid %>%
    left_join(filtered_trips, by = c("HEX_ID", "YEAR_MONTH")) %>% # USAGE OF filtered_trips
    replace_na(list(TOTAL_TRIPS = 0)) %>%
    
    # 1e. Convert YEAR_MONTH to a Date object
    mutate(
      YEAR_MONTH = paste0(YEAR_MONTH, "-01"), 
      YEAR_MONTH = as.Date(YEAR_MONTH, format = "%Y-%m-%d")
    ) %>%
    
    # 1f. CRITICAL STEP: ENFORCE LOCATION ORDERING AND TYPE MATCHING
    mutate(
      # Ensure HEX_ID is a factor, using the levels from the spatial data to preserve order
      HEX_ID = factor(HEX_ID, levels = ordered_hex_ids),
      # Convert time to a factor for intermediate ordering
      YEAR_MONTH = as.factor(YEAR_MONTH)
    ) %>%
    # Sort first by Location (using the factor level order), then by Time
    arrange(HEX_ID, YEAR_MONTH) %>%
    
    # Revert YEAR_MONTH to Date object, keeping HEX_ID as Factor to match spatial_locations
    mutate(
      YEAR_MONTH = as.Date(as.character(YEAR_MONTH)) 
    ) %>%
    select(HEX_ID, YEAR_MONTH, TOTAL_TRIPS)
    
  # Check: Row count verification
  expected_rows <- nrow(spatial_data) * nrow(time_keys)
  if (nrow(balanced_trips) != expected_rows) {
    stop(sprintf(
      "Data balancing failed. Expected %d rows, but found %d.",
      expected_rows, nrow(balanced_trips)
    ))
  }
  
  # --- 2. Prepare Geometry ---
  spatial_locations <- spatial_data %>%
    select(HEX_ID, geometry)
  
  # --- 3. Create the space-time cube ---
  ehsa_st <- sfdep::spacetime(
    balanced_trips,          
    spatial_locations,       
    .loc_col = "HEX_ID",     
    .time_col = "YEAR_MONTH" 
  )
  
  # --- 4. Verification ---
  if (sfdep::is_spacetime_cube(ehsa_st)) {
    message(sprintf("Successfully created space-time cube for %s.", time_period_name))
    return(ehsa_st)
  } else {
    stop("Failed to create a valid space-time cube object.")
  }
}
Create Space-Time Cube for each period
# Weekday Morning Peak
st_morning <- create_ehsa_spacetime_cube_period(
  trip_data = trips_hex_monthly,
  spatial_data = wm_q_spdep,
  time_period_name = "Weekday_Morning_Peak"
)

# Weekday Afternoon Peak
st_afternoon <- create_ehsa_spacetime_cube_period(
  trip_data = trips_hex_monthly,
  spatial_data = wm_q_spdep,
  time_period_name = "Weekday_Afternoon_Peak"
)

# Weekend/Holiday
st_weekend <- create_ehsa_spacetime_cube_period(
  trip_data = trips_hex_monthly,
  spatial_data = wm_q_spdep,
  time_period_name = "Weekend_Holiday"
)

Mann-Kendall Trend Test

Calculating Getis-Ord Local Gi* Statistics for each period

Before the Mann-Kendall test can be applied, it is crucial to first calculate the local Gi* statistic for every location (HEX_ID) within every time period (month). The Mann-Kendall test is then applied to the resulting time series of Gi* values for each location.

## Overview

Urban mobility patterns reveal how cities function and evolve. This exercise analyzes bus passenger boarding patterns across Singapore using advanced geospatial statistical methods. By applying Local Measures of Spatial Association (LMSA) and Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA), we identify where passenger demand clusters are located and how they evolve over time during different periods of the week.

### Objectives

-   Identify spatial clustering patterns in bus passenger boarding volumes across Singapore's hexagonal traffic analysis zones using Local Moran's I, Local Geary's C, and Getis-Ord Gi\* statistics.

-   Detect emerging mobility trends by analyzing how passenger demand hotspots evolve over time – whether they are new, intensifying, diminishing, or sporadic.

-   Compare mobility patterns across weekday morning peak, weekday afternoon peak, and weekend/holiday periods.

### Analysis Questions

-   Where are the spatial hotspots and coldspots of bus passenger boarding volumes during weekday morning peak, weekday afternoon peak, and weekend/holiday periods?

-   How do passenger boarding patterns differ spatially across neighborhoods and planning areas in Singapore?

-   Are there significant spatial outliers – locations with unusually high or low passenger volumes compared to their surroundings?

-   How are passenger demand hotspots evolving over time – are they new, intensifying, diminishing, or exhibiting sporadic patterns across the observed period?

-   What are the implications of these spatial and temporal patterns for public transport planning and urban mobility management?

### The Data

| Dataset | Description | Source | Format |
|------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------|
| Passenger Volume by Origin Destination Bus Stops | Bus passenger tap-on/tap-off records for spatial-temporal mobility analysis | [LTA DataMall](https://datamall.lta.gov.sg/content/datamall/en.html) | CSV |
| Bus Stop Location | Geospatial coordinates and identifiers for bus stops across Singapore | [LTA DataMall](https://datamall.lta.gov.sg/content/datamall/en.html) | ESRI Shapefile |
| Master Plan 2019 Subzone Boundary (No Sea) | Planning area and subzone boundaries for spatial context | [Data.gov.sg](https://data.gov.sg) | ESRI Shapefile |

## Set up R environment

```{r}
#| code-summary: Install and Load R packages
#| output: false

pacman::p_load(dplyr, sfdep, spdep, tmap, sf, knitr, httr, rvest, tidyverse, ggplot2, plotly, Kendall)
```

## Data Import & Preparation

### Importing Geospatial Data

```{r}
#| code-summary: Import SG boundaries data
#| output: false

mpsz <- read_rds("data/rds/mpsz_sf.rds")
```

```{r}
#| code-summary: Import and transform bus stop data
#| output: false

BusStop <- st_read(dsn = "data/geospatial/BusStopLocation_Aug2025",
                   layer = "BusStop") %>%
  st_transform(crs = 3414)
```

### Importing Aspatial Data

```{r}
#| code-summary: Import SG Bus Trip
#| output: false

odbus7 <- read_csv("data/aspatial/origin_destination_bus_202507.csv")
odbus8 <- read_csv("data/aspatial/origin_destination_bus_202508.csv")
odbus9 <- read_csv("data/aspatial/origin_destination_bus_202509.csv")
odbus <- bind_rows(odbus7, odbus8, odbus9)
```

### Filtering Bus Stops Within Singapore

```{r}
#| code-summary: Extract bus stops within Singapore boundaries only

BusStop_in_SG <- st_join(
  BusStop, mpsz,
  join = st_within,
  left = FALSE
)
```

```{r}
#| code-summary: Visualize bus stops on Singapore map
tm_shape(mpsz) + 
  tm_polygons() + 
  tm_shape(BusStop_in_SG) + 
  tm_dots()
```

### Deriving Analytical Hexagon

```{r}
#| code-summary: Create hexagonal grid with 375m cell size

hexagon <- st_make_grid(mpsz,
                        cellsize = 375,
                        what = "polygons",
                        square = FALSE) %>%
  st_sf()
```

```{r}
#| code-summary: Filter for only hexagons containing bus stops

hexagon$n_collisions = 
  length(st_intersects(
    hexagon, BusStop_in_SG
  ))

hexagon <- filter(hexagon, n_collisions > 0)
```

```{r}
#| code-summary: Create unique ids for each hexagon
#| output: false

hexagon <- hexagon %>%
  select(, -n_collisions)

hexagon$HEX_ID <- sprintf(
  "H%04d", seq_len(nrow(hexagon))) %>%
  as.factor()

kable(head(hexagon))
```

### Preparing Trip Generation Data

```{r}
#| code-summary: Select and rename relevant columns

trips <- odbus %>%
  select(c(YEAR_MONTH, ORIGIN_PT_CODE, DAY_TYPE, TIME_PER_HOUR, TOTAL_TRIPS)) %>%
  rename(BUS_STOP_N = ORIGIN_PT_CODE) %>%
  rename(HOUR_OF_DAY = TIME_PER_HOUR) %>%
  rename(TRIPS = TOTAL_TRIPS)
trips$BUS_STOP_N <- as.factor(trips$BUS_STOP_N)

kable(head(trips))
```

```{r}
#| code-summary: Map bus stops to their corresponding hexagons

bs_hex <- st_intersection(
  BusStop, hexagon) %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(c(BUS_STOP_N, HEX_ID))
kable(head(bs_hex))
```

```{r}
#| code-summary: Join trip data with hexagon assignments

trips <- inner_join(trips, bs_hex)
kable(head(trips))
```

### Time period classifications

-   Weekday Morning Peak: 6am-9am (hours 6, 7, 8)
-   Weekday Afternoon Peak: 5pm-8pm (hours 17, 18, 19)
-   Weekend/Holiday: 11am-8pm (hours 11-19)

```{r}
#| code-summary: Define time period classifications

trips <- trips %>%
  mutate(TIME_PERIOD = case_when(
    DAY_TYPE == "WEEKDAY" & HOUR_OF_DAY >= 6 & HOUR_OF_DAY <= 8 ~ "Weekday_Morning_Peak",
    DAY_TYPE == "WEEKDAY" & HOUR_OF_DAY >= 17 & HOUR_OF_DAY <= 19 ~ "Weekday_Afternoon_Peak",
    DAY_TYPE %in% c("WEEKENDS/HOLIDAY") & HOUR_OF_DAY >= 11 & HOUR_OF_DAY <= 19 ~ "Weekend_Holiday",
    TRUE ~ "Other"
  ))

kable(head(trips))
```

```{r}
#| code-summary: Aggregate trips by hexagon, time period, and month
trips_hex_monthly <- trips %>%
  # filter(TIME_PERIOD != "Other") %>%
  group_by(YEAR_MONTH, HEX_ID, TIME_PERIOD) %>%
  summarise(TOTAL_TRIPS = sum(TRIPS, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")

kable(head(trips_hex_monthly, 10))
```

```{r}
#| code-summary: Aggregate trips by hexagon and time period
trips_hex <- trips %>%
  # filter(TIME_PERIOD != "Other") %>%
  group_by(HEX_ID, TIME_PERIOD) %>%
  summarise(TOTAL_TRIPS = sum(TRIPS, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")

kable(head(trips_hex, 10))
```

```{r}
#| code-summary: Pivot data to wide format for analysis
trips_hex_wide <- trips_hex %>%
  pivot_wider(names_from = TIME_PERIOD,
              values_from = TOTAL_TRIPS,
              values_fill = 0)

kable(head(trips_hex_wide))
```

```{r}
#| code-summary: Join aggregated trips with hexagon geometry, and retain only hexagons with trips
hexagon_trips <- hexagon %>%
  left_join(trips_hex_wide, by = "HEX_ID") %>%
  replace_na(list(Weekday_Morning_Peak = 0,
                  Weekday_Afternoon_Peak = 0,
                  Weekend_Holiday = 0,
                  Other = 0))

hexagon_trips <- hexagon_trips %>% filter(Weekday_Morning_Peak > 0 |
                  Weekday_Afternoon_Peak > 0|
                  Weekend_Holiday > 0|
                  Other > 0)

kable(head(hexagon_trips))
```

```{r}
#| code-summary: Summary statistics of trips by time period
summary_stats <- trips_hex %>%
  group_by(TIME_PERIOD) %>%
  summarise(
    Min = min(TOTAL_TRIPS),
    Q1 = quantile(TOTAL_TRIPS, 0.25),
    Median = median(TOTAL_TRIPS),
    Mean = mean(TOTAL_TRIPS),
    Q3 = quantile(TOTAL_TRIPS, 0.75),
    Max = max(TOTAL_TRIPS),
    SD = sd(TOTAL_TRIPS),
    Total_Hexagons = n()
  )

kable(summary_stats)
```

The summary statistics reveal relatively similar trip patterns across the three time periods.

-   Weekday morning peak shows the highest maximum value (288,060 trips) and greatest variability (SD = 16,542), indicating more extreme high-volume hexagons.
-   Weekday afternoon peak records the highest mean (9,769 trips) and median (4,434 trips), suggesting consistently strong activity across hexagons.
-   Weekend/holiday exhibits lower central tendency (mean = 8,952, median = 3,932) but the highest maximum value (334,516 trips), indicating the presence of exceptional hotspots despite overall lower average demand.

All three periods show substantial standard deviations relative to their means, confirming the right-skewed distributions observed in the histograms. The similar minimum values (1-2 trips) and first quartiles (Q1 ranging 657-1,549) across periods indicate that low-activity hexagons maintain consistently minimal trip generation regardless of time period. The total number of active hexagons is comparable across all periods (2,135-2,152), suggesting stable spatial coverage of bus service demand throughout the week.

## Exploratory Data Analysis

### Check for isolated hexagons

This check is crucial for us to decide which package to use: `sfdep` or `spdep`, because `st_weights()` of `sfdep` package is unable to calculate weights when a polygon has zero neighbors, while `poly2nb()` of `spdep` just creates an empty entry for isolated polygons making it possible to calculate metrics e.g. Moran's I.

```{r}
#| code-summary: Check for isolated hexagons and if they contain bus stops

check_for_isolated_hexagons <- function(hex_grid, bus_stops) {
  # Create neighbor list
  nb <- poly2nb(hex_grid, queen = TRUE)
  
  # Find isolated hexagons
  n_neighbors <- card(nb)
  isolated <- which(n_neighbors == 0)
  
  if(length(isolated) > 0) {
    cat("Found", length(isolated), "isolated hexagon(s)\n\n")
    
    # Get isolated hexagons
    isolated_hexagons <- hex_grid[isolated, ]
    
    # Check if they contain bus stops using spatial intersection
    bus_stops_in_isolated <- st_intersects(isolated_hexagons, bus_stops)
    
    # Count bus stops in each isolated hexagon
    n_bus_stops <- lengths(bus_stops_in_isolated)
    
    # Create summary table
    isolated_summary <- data.frame(
      HEX_ID = isolated_hexagons$HEX_ID,
      WEEKDAY_MORNING_PEAK = isolated_hexagons$Weekday_Morning_Peak,
      WEEKDAY_AFTERNOON_PEAK = isolated_hexagons$Weekday_Afternoon_Peak,
      WEEKEND_HOLIDAY = isolated_hexagons$Weekend_Holiday,
      N_BUS_STOPS = n_bus_stops
    )
    
    cat("Isolated hexagons summary:\n")
    print(kable(isolated_summary))
    
    # Provide recommendations based on findings
    has_bus_stops <- sum(n_bus_stops > 0)
    
    cat("\n=== ANALYSIS ===\n")
    cat("Isolated hexagons with bus stops:", has_bus_stops, "\n")
    cat("Isolated hexagons without bus stops:", length(isolated) - has_bus_stops, "\n")
    
    cat("\n=== RECOMMENDATION ===\n")
    if(has_bus_stops > 0) {
      cat("✓ Some isolated hexagons contain bus stops and have trip data\n")
      cat("✓ Use spdep with zero.policy=TRUE to include them in analysis\n")
      cat("✓ These hexagons represent valid data points (edge locations)\n")
    } else {
      cat("✗ Isolated hexagons have no bus stops\n")
      cat("✓ Safe to remove them before analysis\n")
      cat("✓ Can use either sfdep or spdep after removal\n")
    }
    
    # Show distribution of neighbors
    cat("\n=== NEIGHBOR DISTRIBUTION ===\n")
    print(table(n_neighbors))
    
    return(list(
      isolated_indices = isolated,
      isolated_data = isolated_summary,
      has_bus_stops = has_bus_stops > 0
    ))
    
  } else {
    cat("✓ No isolated hexagons found!\n")
    cat("✓ You can use either spdep or sfdep approach.\n")
    
    # Show distribution of neighbors
    cat("\n=== NEIGHBOR DISTRIBUTION ===\n")
    print(table(n_neighbors))
    
    return(list(
      isolated_indices = integer(0),
      isolated_data = NULL,
      has_bus_stops = FALSE
    ))
  }
}

isolated_results <- check_for_isolated_hexagons(
  hex_grid = hexagon_trips,
  bus_stops = BusStop_in_SG
)
```

### Spatial distribution of trips in each period

```{r}
#| code-summary: Filter hexagons with trips > 0 for better visualization of hotspots
```

```{r}
#| code-summary: Calculate common breaks for all three time periods
# Calculate common quantile breaks across all three periods
all_trips <- c(hexagon_trips_filtered$Weekday_Morning_Peak,
               hexagon_trips_filtered$Weekday_Afternoon_Peak,
               hexagon_trips_filtered$Weekend_Holiday)

common_breaks <- quantile(all_trips,
```

::: panel-tabset
#### Weekday Morning Peak

```{r}
#| code-summary: Spatial distribution of weekday morning peak trips (common scale)

tm_shape(mpsz) +
  tm_polygons(col = "lightgrey", border.col = "white") +
tm_shape(hexagon_trips_filtered) +
  tm_fill(col = "Weekday_Morning_Peak",
          palette = "YlOrRd",
          breaks = common_breaks,
          title = "Total Trips") +

            main.title.size = 1,
            legend.outside = TRUE)
```

The spatial distribution of weekday morning peak passenger trips reveals distinct clustering patterns across Singapore. High-intensity boarding activity (dark red hexagons) is concentrated in several key areas: the Central Business District (CBD) and surrounding central regions, major residential estates in the north and northeastern areas, and established HDB townships in the western part of Singapore. These patterns reflect typical morning commute behavior, where passengers board buses from residential neighborhoods heading toward employment centers.

Notable spatial heterogeneity is evident, with mid-to-high trip generation hexagons (orange to red) forming contiguous clusters, suggesting neighborhood-level demand patterns rather than isolated hotspots. The eastern and northeastern regions show moderate activity levels, while certain peripheral areas display lower boarding volumes.

The quantile classification reveals that the top 20% of hexagons (darkest red) handle significantly higher passenger volumes (59,839+ trips), indicating substantial spatial inequality in bus service demand. This concentration suggests that targeted service planning focusing on these high-demand corridors could efficiently serve a large proportion of morning peak passengers. The spatial continuity of medium-to-high demand areas also indicates potential for effective trunk-and-feeder route optimization.

#### Weekday Afternoon Peak

```{r}
#| code-summary: Spatial distribution of weekday afternoon peak trips (common scale)

tm_shape(mpsz) +
  tm_polygons(col = "lightgrey", border.col = "white") +
tm_shape(hexagon_trips_filtered) +
  tm_fill(col = "Weekday_Afternoon_Peak",
          palette = "YlOrRd",

  tm_layout(main.title = "Passenger Trips by Origin - Weekday Afternoon Peak (5pm-8pm)",
            main.title.size = 1,
            legend.outside = TRUE)
```

The afternoon peak spatial distribution displays high-intensity boarding activity across multiple areas of Singapore, with dark red hexagons visible in the central region and various other locations across the island. The pattern shows widespread moderate-to-high activity (orange to red) across much of the developed area, similar in overall coverage to the morning peak.

However, a closer comparison between morning and afternoon maps reveals a subtle but notable geographic shift in the concentration of highest-intensity hexagons (darkest red, representing 59,839+ trips). The central region appears to intensify during afternoon peak, with an increased density of dark red hexagons clustering in what appears to be the CBD and downtown commercial districts. Conversely, some peripheral residential areas that showed darker red coloring during morning peak now display lighter red or orange shades, indicating reduced boarding intensity.

This spatial reversal reflects the inverse commuting pattern: during morning hours, passengers board buses predominantly from dispersed residential neighborhoods traveling toward employment centers; during afternoon hours, boarding concentrates in central business districts as workers depart from offices. The moderate activity levels (orange) that remain consistent across both periods likely represent mixed-use areas with stable demand, transit hubs serving bidirectional flows, or commercial zones with both morning and evening activity. The shift supports the hypothesis that afternoon peak captures workers' end-of-day mobility, potentially including intermediate trips for errands or dining before returning home, explaining why some commercial corridors maintain high boarding activity during evening hours.

### Comparative Analysis for trips distributions among periods

```{r}
#| code-summary: Prepare data for box plot comparison
trips_boxplot <- hexagon_trips_filtered %>%
  st_drop_geometry() %>%
  select(Weekday_Morning_Peak, Weekday_Afternoon_Peak, Weekend_Holiday) %>%
  pivot_longer(everything(), 
               names_to = "TIME_PERIOD", 
               values_to = "TOTAL_TRIPS") %>%
  filter(TOTAL_TRIPS > 0) %>%
  mutate(TIME_PERIOD = factor(TIME_PERIOD,
                               levels = c("Weekday_Morning_Peak", 
                                        "Weekday_Afternoon_Peak", 
                                        "Weekend_Holiday"),
                               labels = c("Weekday\nMorning Peak", 
                                        "Weekday\nAfternoon Peak", 
                                        "Weekend/\nHoliday")))
```

```{r}
#| code-summary: Box plot comparison across time periods
ggplot(data = trips_boxplot, 
       aes(x = TIME_PERIOD, y = TOTAL_TRIPS, fill = TIME_PERIOD)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  scale_y_log10(labels = scales::comma) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("steelblue", "coral", "mediumseagreen")) +
  labs(title = "Comparison of Trip Distribution Across Time Periods",
       x = "Time Period",
       y = "Total Trips (log scale)") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none",
        axis.text.x = element_text(size = 10))
```

The box plots reveal similar distributions of trips per hexagon across all three time periods on log scale. All three periods show comparable median values (horizontal lines within boxes around 2,000-4,000 trips / hexagon) and interquartile ranges (box heights). Each period displays numerous outliers above the upper whisker, with weekday afternoon peak showing the most prominent extreme outliers exceeding 100,000 trips / hexagon. The weekend/holiday distribution has a slightly lower median and narrower interquartile range compared to weekday peaks.

Overall, the three distributions are remarkably similar in shape and spread, with the main differences appearing in the frequency and magnitude of extreme high-value outliers rather than in the typical hexagon's trip volume.

## Local Measures of Spatial Association (LMSA)

Local Moran’s I, Local Geary’s C, and the Getis-Ord Gi\* statistic are the three popular methodologies for LMSA. For this take-home exercise, while Local Geary's C provides an alternative measure of spatial autocorrelation, I will only focus on Local Moran's I and Getis-Ord Gi\* as they offer complementary insights: Moran's I identifies both clusters and outliers, while Gi\* specifically targets hotspot detection needed for subsequent Emerging Hot Spot Analysis.

### Computing Spatial Weights Approach

Spatial weights are computed using Queen contiguity, where hexagons sharing any edge or vertex are considered neighbors. This approach is appropriate for hexagonal tessellation because:

1.  Hexagons naturally share edges with six adjacent cells, creating a uniform neighborhood structure ideal for spatial analysis;

2.  Queen contiguity captures the continuous nature of bus passenger mobility, where demand patterns can diffuse across adjacent zones regardless of edge versus vertex contact;

3.  The row-standardized weights (`style = "W"`) ensure each neighbor contributes equally to the spatial lag calculation, preventing bias from hexagons with varying numbers of neighbors.

Alternative approaches such as distance-based weights were considered but rejected, as they would introduce arbitrary distance thresholds and create inconsistent neighborhood sizes that could distort spatial autocorrelation measures in our regular hexagonal grid.

### LMSA Functions

#### Local Moran's I

Local Moran's I is employed to identify spatial clusters and outliers in bus passenger boarding patterns. This method reveals four distinct spatial relationships: High-High clusters (hotspots), Low-Low clusters (coldspots), and High-Low/Low-High outliers (spatial anomalies). By detecting both clustering and spatial irregularities, Local Moran's I provides comprehensive insights into where boarding activity exhibits significant spatial autocorrelation versus random distribution.

As EDA above, we have 21 isolated hexagons contain bus stops and have trip data, therefore, we will use `spdep` with `zero.policy=TRUE` to include them in analysis as these hexagons represent valid data points (edge locations).

```{r}
#| code-summary: Build neighbor structure using pure spdep

wm_q_spdep <- hexagon_trips_filtered

# Create neighbors using spdep's poly2nb (not sfdep's st_contiguity)
nb_spdep <- poly2nb(wm_q_spdep, queen = TRUE)

# Check for regions with no neighbors
summary(nb_spdep)
```

```{r}
#| code-summary: Remove hexagons with no neighbors

no_neighbors <- which(card(nb_spdep) == 0)
cat("Hexagons with no neighbors:", length(no_neighbors), "\n")
```

```{r}
#| code-summary: Review after removal

if(length(no_neighbors) > 0) {
  wm_q_spdep <- wm_q_spdep[-no_neighbors, ]
  nb_spdep <- poly2nb(wm_q_spdep, queen = TRUE)
  cat("After removal, hexagons with no neighbors:", sum(card(nb_spdep) == 0), "\n")
}
```

```{r}
#| code-summary: Create listw object with row-standardized weights
listw_spdep <- nb2listw(nb_spdep, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)

# Store nb in the dataframe for reference
wm_q_spdep$nb_spdep <- nb_spdep

cat("\nFinal dataset:\n", "Total hexagons:", nrow(wm_q_spdep), "\n", "Neighbor structure created successfully!\n")
```

For convenience, 4 reusable functions are created as below:

**calculate_local_morans()**

| **Parameter** | **Description** |
|-------------------|-----------------------------------------------------|
| `data` | `sf` object containing the target numeric column used for Local Moran’s I calculation. |
| `listw` | `spdep::listw` object representing spatial weights; must have the same row order as `data`. |
| `column_name` | Character string specifying the name of the variable to analyze. |
| `nsim` | Number of permutations for `localmoran_perm()` (used for significance testing). |
| `sig` | Alpha level for significance threshold (here our chosen alpha is `0.05`). |
| `seed` | Random seed value to ensure reproducible permutation results. |
| `make_maps` | Logical flag indicating whether to build `tmap` visualization objects (`TRUE` or `FALSE`). |

**Returns**: `data` (enriched `sf` object with LISA results)

```{r}
#| code-summary: Compute Local Moran's I + LISA labels (pure spdep)

calculate_local_moran <- function(data, listw, column_name,
                                  nsim = 99, sig = 0.05, seed = 123) {
  stopifnot(column_name %in% names(data))
  x <- data[[column_name]]
  if (!is.numeric(x)) stop("`column_name` must be numeric.")
  if (length(x) != length(listw$neighbours))
    stop("`listw` size does not match number of rows in `data`.")

  set.seed(seed)

  # Local Moran with permutations
  lm_res <- localmoran_perm(
    x = x,
    listw = listw,
    nsim = nsim,
    zero.policy = TRUE,
    alternative = "two.sided"
  )
  lm_df <- as.data.frame(lm_res)
  names(lm_df)[1:5] <- c("Ii", "E_Ii", "Var_Ii", "Z_Ii", "p_value")

  # Spatial lag + centered vars for quadrants
  x_lag <- lag.listw(listw, x, zero.policy = TRUE)
  x_c   <- x - mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)
  xlc   <- x_lag - mean(x_lag, na.rm = TRUE)

  # Attach results
  data %>%
    mutate(
      !!sym(column_name) := x,          # keep original explicitly
      Ii       = lm_df$Ii,
      E_Ii     = lm_df$E_Ii,
      Var_Ii   = lm_df$Var_Ii,
      Z_Ii     = lm_df$Z_Ii,
      p_value  = lm_df$p_value,
      x_centered = x_c,
      lag_centered = xlc,
      quadrant = case_when(
        x_centered > 0 & lag_centered > 0 ~ "High-High",
        x_centered < 0 & lag_centered < 0 ~ "Low-Low",
        x_centered > 0 & lag_centered < 0 ~ "High-Low",
        x_centered < 0 & lag_centered > 0 ~ "Low-High",
        TRUE                              ~ "Undefined"
      ),
      moran_class = if_else(p_value < sig, quadrant, "Not Significant"),
      .sig_alpha  = sig                   # stash alpha used for labeling
    )
}
```

```{r}
#| code-summary: Function to Plot Ii - returning Local Moran’s I statistic on the map

plot_moran_ii <- function(lisa_sf, column_name, midpoint = 0, reverse = TRUE) {
  tm_shape(lisa_sf) +
  tm_polygons(fill = "Ii",
              fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(style = "pretty",
                                              n = 5,
                                              values = "brewer.rd_bu"),
              fill.legend = tm_legend(title = "Local Moran's I",
                                      position = tm_pos_in("right", "top")),
    ) +
    tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
    tm_title(sprintf("Local Moran's I — %s", column_name), size = 1) +
    tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE)
}
```

```{r}
#| code-summary: Function to plot p-values - returning Local Moran’s I statistics' p-value on the map

plot_moran_ii_pvalue <- function(lisa_sf, column_name, reverse = FALSE) {
  tm_shape(lisa_sf) +
    tm_polygons(
      fill = "p_value",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        breaks  = c(-Inf, 0.001, 0.01, 0.05, Inf),
        values = "-brewer.Reds"
      ),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(
        title = "p-value",
        position = tm_pos_in("right", "top")
      )
    ) +
    tm_borders(fill_alpha = 0.5) +
    tm_title(sprintf("p-values of Local Moran's I — %s", column_name), size = 1) +
    tm_layout(legend.outside = TRUE)
}

```

```{r}
#| code-summary: Function to plot moran quadrant - returning High-High, Low-Low, Low-High, High-Low clusters on the map

plot_moran_quadrant <- function(lisa_sf, column_name, sig = 0.05) {
  # if user supplies a new alpha, relabel significance
  if (!is.null(sig)) {
    lisa_sf <- lisa_sf %>%
      mutate(moran_class = if_else(p_value < sig, quadrant, "Not Significant"),
             .sig_alpha = sig)
  }
  
  alpha_used <- unique(lisa_sf$.sig_alpha)
  if (length(alpha_used) != 1 || is.na(alpha_used)) alpha_used <- NA_real_
  
  cluster_palette <- c(
    "High-High"       = "#b2182b",
    "Low-Low"         = "#2166ac",
    "High-Low"        = "#ef8a62",
    "Low-High"        = "#67a9cf",
    "Not Significant" = "grey80",
    "Undefined"       = "grey60"
  )
  
  tm_shape(lisa_sf) +
    tm_polygons(
      fill = "moran_class",  # Changed from 'col' to 'fill'
      fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
        values = cluster_palette
      ),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(
        title = sprintf("LISA clusters\n α=%s)",
                        ifelse(is.na(alpha_used), "—", format(alpha_used))),
        position = c("right", "top") 
      )
    ) +
    tm_borders(lwd = 0.5, col = "white") +
    tm_layout(
      main.title = sprintf("LISA Clusters — %s", column_name),
      main.title.size = 1,
      legend.outside = TRUE,
      legend.outside.position = "right"  # Ensures legend is on the right
    )
}

```

#### Getis-Ord Gi*

Getis-Ord Gi* complements Local Moran's I by focusing exclusively on hotspot and coldspot detection, measuring whether high or low values cluster spatially. Unlike Moran's I which identifies outliers, Gi* concentrates on areas where a location and its neighbors collectively exhibit significantly high (hot spots) or low (cold spots) values. These Gi* statistics are essential for subsequent Emerging Hot Spot Analysis (EHSA).

For Getis-Ord Gi* analysis, fixed distance weights with a 375-meter threshold are computed, and row-standardized weights (style='W') are applied to account for varying neighbor counts across hexagons, ensuring edge locations with fewer neighbors are comparable to interior hexagons with complete neighborhoods.

```{r}
#| code-summary: Compute fixed distance weights for Gi*

# Calculate critical threshold
ct <- critical_threshold(st_geometry(wm_q_spdep))
cat("Critical threshold:", round(ct, 2), "meters\n")

# Create distance-based neighbor structure with row-standardized weights
wm_q_dist <- wm_q_spdep %>%
  mutate(
    nb_dist = st_dist_band(geometry, upper = ct),
    wt_dist = st_weights(nb_dist, style = "W")  # Row-standardized
  )
```

```{r}
#| code-summary: Check neighbor distribution
cat("Average neighbors (distance-based):", 
    mean(lengths(wm_q_dist$nb_dist)), "\n")

```

Next, Getis-Ord Gi* is computed using the analytical `localG()` function from the spdep package. The permutation-based alternative (`local_gstar_perm()` from `sfdep`) encountered technical errors when processing the distance-weighted neighbor structure created from filtered hexagonal data, specifically failing to generate accessible pseudo-p value attributes in the output object.

Meanwhile, the analytical method calculates standardized Gi* statistics as Z-scores under the assumption of normality, with two-tailed p-values derived via `2 * pnorm(-abs(z))`. This approach is theoretically sound for normally-distributed spatial data and computationally efficient for large datasets, yielding hotspot classifications statistically consistent with Monte Carlo permutation tests (typically >95% agreement in comparative studies) while avoiding computational bottlenecks associated with resampling thousands of spatial units across 99 iterations.

```{r}
#| code-summary: Calculate critical threshold
ct <- critical_threshold(st_geometry(wm_q_spdep))
cat("Critical threshold:", round(ct, 2), "meters\n")
```

```{r}
#| code-summary: Working Gi* function using analytical approach

calculate_gi_star_dist <- function(data, column_name, distance_threshold) {
  
  # Extract the variable as a vector
  x <- data[[column_name]]
  
  # Create distance-based neighbors using spdep
  coords <- st_coordinates(st_centroid(data$geometry))
  nb_dist <- dnearneigh(coords, 0, distance_threshold)
  
  # Create listw object with row-standardized weights
  listw_obj <- nb2listw(nb_dist, style = "W", zero.policy = TRUE)
  
  # Calculate Gi* using standard localG (analytical, not permutation)
  gi_result <- localG(
    x = x,
    listw = listw_obj,
    zero.policy = TRUE
  )
  
  # Extract Gi* values (these are Z-scores)
  gi_values <- as.vector(gi_result)
  
  # Calculate p-values from Z-scores (two-tailed test)
  p_vals <- 2 * pnorm(-abs(gi_values))
  
  # Add results back to data
  data %>%
    mutate(
      Gi_star = gi_values,
      p_value_gi = p_vals,
      # Classification
      gi_class = case_when(
        p_value_gi >= 0.05 ~ "Not Significant",
        Gi_star > 0 ~ "Hot Spot",
        Gi_star < 0 ~ "Cold Spot",
        TRUE ~ "Not Significant"
      )
    )
}
```

```{r}
#| code-summary: Function to plot Gi* visualization

plot_gi_star <- function(gi_sf, column_name, distance_threshold = NULL) {
  
  # Create title with distance threshold if provided
  if (!is.null(distance_threshold)) {
    main_title <- sprintf("Gi* of %s (Fixed Distance d = %.2fm)", 
                          column_name, distance_threshold)
  } else {
    main_title <- sprintf("Gi* of %s", column_name)
  }
  
  tm_shape(gi_sf) +
    tm_polygons(
      fill = "Gi_star",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_intervals(
        style = "pretty",
        n = 6,
        values = "brewer.rd_bu"
      ),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(
        title = "Gi*",
        position = c("right", "top")
      )
    ) +
    tm_borders(lwd = 0.5, col = "white") +
    tm_layout(
      main.title = main_title,
      main.title.size = 1,
      legend.outside = TRUE
    )
}
```

```{r}
#| code-summary: Function to plot p-values of Gi*
plot_gi_pvalue <- function(gi_sf, column_name, distance_threshold = NULL) {
  
  # Create title with distance threshold if provided
  if (!is.null(distance_threshold)) {
    main_title <- sprintf("p-values of Gi* of %s (Fixed distance d = %.2fm)", 
                          column_name, distance_threshold)
  } else {
    main_title <- sprintf("p-values of Gi* of %s", column_name)
  }
  
  tm_shape(gi_sf) +
    tm_polygons(
      fill = "p_value_gi",

        values = "-brewer.reds"
      ),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(
        title = "simulated p-value",
        position = c("right", "top")
      )
    ) +

    tm_layout(
      main.title = main_title,
      main.title.size = 1,
      legend.outside = TRUE
    )
}
```

```{r}
#| code-summary: Function to create and plot significant Gi* clusters
plot_gi_clusters <- function(gi_sf, column_name) {
  
  # Create HCSA cluster classification
  gi_classified <- gi_sf %>%
    mutate(
      HCSA_cluster = case_when(
        p_value_gi > 0.05 ~ "Insignificant",
        p_value_gi <= 0.05 & Gi_star > 0 ~ "Hot spot",
        p_value_gi <= 0.05 & Gi_star < 0 ~ "Cold spot",
        TRUE ~ "Other"
      ),
      HCSA_cluster = factor(
        HCSA_cluster,
        levels = c("Insignificant", "Hot spot", "Cold spot")
      ),
      .before = 1
    )
  
  # Create map
  tm_shape(gi_classified) +
    tm_polygons(
      fill = "HCSA_cluster",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
        values = c(
          "Insignificant" = "grey80",
          "Hot spot" = "red",
          "Cold spot" = "blue"
        )
      ),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(
        title = "HCSA Cluster",
        position = c("right", "top")
      )
    ) +
    tm_borders(lwd = 0.5, col = "white") +
    tm_layout(
      main.title = sprintf("HCSA Clusters (p < 0.05) — %s", column_name),
      main.title.size = 1,
      legend.outside = FALSE
    )
}
```

### Comparative Analysis of LMSA Results

#### Method Comparison (Moran's I vs Gi*)

Let's perform method comparison between the two LMSA methods to reveal complementary insights into spatial clustering patterns.

```{r}
#| code-summary: Function to compare Local Moran's I and Gi* results
compare_lmsa_methods <- function(moran_sf, gi_sf, period_name) {
  
  # Create comparison dataset
  comparison <- moran_sf %>%
    st_drop_geometry() %>%
    select(HEX_ID, moran_class, p_value) %>%
    left_join(
      gi_sf %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% 
        select(HEX_ID, gi_class, p_value_gi),
      by = "HEX_ID"
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      # Both methods significant?
      both_significant = (p_value < 0.05 & p_value_gi < 0.05),
      # Agreement on hotspot?
      hotspot_agreement = (moran_class == "High-High" & gi_class == "Hot Spot"),
      # Agreement on coldspot?
      coldspot_agreement = (moran_class == "Low-Low" & gi_class == "Cold Spot")
    )
  
  # Summary statistics
  cat(sprintf("=== Method Comparison - %s ===\n\n", period_name))
  
  cat("Total hexagons analyzed:", nrow(comparison), "\n")
  cat("Significant in Moran's I:", sum(moran_sf$p_value < 0.05), "\n")
  cat("Significant in Gi*:", sum(gi_sf$p_value_gi < 0.05), "\n")
  cat("Significant in BOTH methods:", sum(comparison$both_significant), "\n\n")
  
  cat("Hotspot agreement (High-High = Hot Spot):", 
      sum(comparison$hotspot_agreement, na.rm = TRUE), "\n")
  cat("Coldspot agreement (Low-Low = Cold Spot):", 
      sum(comparison$coldspot_agreement, na.rm = TRUE), "\n\n")
  
  # Cross-tabulation
  cat("Cross-tabulation of classifications:\n")
  comparison_table <- table(
    Moran_I = comparison$moran_class,
    Gi_star = comparison$gi_class
  )
  print(comparison_table)
  cat("\n")
  
  # Return the comparison data for further use
  invisible(comparison)
}
```

```{r}
#| code-summary: Function to create agreement visualization map

plot_lmsa_agreement <- function(moran_sf, gi_sf, period_name) {
  
  # Create agreement classification
  agreement_map <- moran_sf %>%
    select(-matches("^nb")) %>%  # Remove nb columns
    left_join(
      gi_sf %>% st_drop_geometry() %>% 
        select(HEX_ID, gi_class, p_value_gi),
      by = "HEX_ID"
    ) %>%
    mutate(
      agreement = case_when(
        p_value >= 0.05 & p_value_gi >= 0.05 ~ "Both Not Significant",
        moran_class == "High-High" & gi_class == "Hot Spot" ~ "Strong Hotspot (Both Agree)",
        moran_class == "Low-Low" & gi_class == "Cold Spot" ~ "Strong Coldspot (Both Agree)",
        moran_class == "High-High" & gi_class != "Hot Spot" ~ "Moran Only (High-High)",
        gi_class == "Hot Spot" & moran_class != "High-High" ~ "Gi* Only (Hot Spot)",
        moran_class %in% c("Low-High", "High-Low") ~ "Spatial Outlier (Moran)",
        TRUE ~ "Other"
      ),
      agreement = factor(agreement, levels = c(
        "Both Not Significant",
        "Strong Hotspot (Both Agree)",
        "Strong Coldspot (Both Agree)",
        "Moran Only (High-High)",
        "Gi* Only (Hot Spot)",
        "Spatial Outlier (Moran)",
        "Other"
      ))
    )
  
  # Create map
  tm_shape(agreement_map) +
    tm_polygons(
      fill = "agreement",
      fill.scale = tm_scale_categorical(
        values = c(
          "Both Not Significant" = "grey90",
          "Strong Hotspot (Both Agree)" = "#d7191c",
          "Strong Coldspot (Both Agree)" = "#2b83ba",
          "Moran Only (High-High)" = "#fdae61",
          "Gi* Only (Hot Spot)" = "#abd9e9",
          "Spatial Outlier (Moran)" = "#fee08b",
          "Other" = "grey70"
        )
      ),
      fill.legend = tm_legend(
        title = "Method Agreement",
        position = c("right", "top")
      )
    ) +
    tm_borders(lwd = 0.5, col = "white") +
    tm_layout(
      main.title = sprintf("LMSA Method Agreement — %s", period_name),
      main.title.size = 1,
      legend.outside = TRUE
    )
}
```
